dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Read kernel.py, problem.py, submission_tests.py; extracted VLEN=8, N_CORES=1, exact SLOT_LIMITS, SCRATCH_SIZE, full instruction set, and high-level forest/rounds/hash-stage computation before editing.
Small probing experiments confirming vector op and multiply_add semantics and arithmetic-selection correctness — confirming ambiguous behavior empirically rather than guessing.
Discovered/re-derived precise simulator semantics: all slots in a bundle see pre-bundle state (RAW hazard), load slot limit of 2 causes crashes — accurate cost/hazard model of bundle execution.
Re-read problem.py mid-optimization to re-examine load_offset (mem[scratch[addr+offset]]) semantics when seeking gather optimizations — orientation refined as new unknowns surfaced.
Built a working hazard-tracking VLIW scheduler and repeatedly tied the machine model to theoretical cycle floors (~2048 load-limited, ~1245 with level pre-loading).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read all relevant sources and built a precise, explicit model of slots/units, per-bundle cost rules (2-load limit, pre-bundle read semantics), hash-stage dependencies (stage 0/2/4 fusion), SIMD width, and the reference contract, confirming ambiguous behavior with targeted small experiments (multiply_add, arithmetic select, scheduler) and re-probing problem.py when surprised — squarely matching anchor 8. It stops short of 10 because it never consolidated a complete instruction-latency/slot-contention spec, and orientation, though continuously refined, was tangled with heavy thrash rather than a cleanly converging operational spec.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates

evidence.note: Articulates an ordered milestone plan (vectorize → multiply_add fusion → pack bundles → pipeline) with rough per-stage cycle targets (6.8x→21821, 13.3x→11091), matching a sensible staged decomposition.
Re-derives the load-slot floor (~2048 cycles) and re-prioritizes the plan toward level pre-loading to eliminate loads — decomposition evolving with measured evidence, pushing above anchor 5.
Repeatedly states an incremental 'add one optimization at a time, test between each step' milestone plan with correctness gates — strong stated structure.

Despite the incremental plan, it keeps writing big multi-optimization rewrites that fail and get reverted, entangling correctness and speed changes rather than landing/measuring each transform independently — the milestone discipline is not sustained.
Ends still at ~9356 cycles cycling through interleaving rewrites; the ordered plan never resolves into independently gated, measured milestones.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 3 and meets anchor 5: it lays out a sensible ordered plan (correct rewrite → vectorize → pack → pipeline) with rough per-stage cycle targets and verifies at points, and it goes further by re-prioritizing the decomposition around the empirically-discovered load-slot bottleneck (toward anchor 10's evidence-adjusted decomposition). However, it falls short of anchor 8 because the stated 'one transform at a time, gated by correctness' discipline is repeatedly abandoned in favor of entangled big-bang rewrites that fail and revert, so transforms are not actually landed and measured independently. Averaging strong, evidence-adjusted plan articulation against weak sustained milestone execution lands the observed level at 6.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test

evidence.note: Runs run_tests.sh after each new kernel version, confirming both correctness and cycle count at every stage — clearly exceeds the 'occasional' anchor-3 behavior and meets anchor-5's 're-check after each optimization stage'.
Isolates the multiply_add hash-fusion transform and verifies it mathematically/empirically before relying on it — the anchor-8 'isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results' behavior.

Builds standalone test scripts for the binary-selection algorithm and a VLIW hazard-tracking scheduler, and later catches a selection-pairing bug via testing — self-built checks beyond the canonical test.
Explicitly guards against VLIW-specific corruption (same-bundle RAW hazards, wrong node index) and detects these correctness bugs through testing rather than assuming transforms are safe.

Relies on run_tests.sh (which covers randomized inputs) for robustness confirmation rather than constructing its own varied-input reference diff — the reason it falls short of anchors 8-10's disciplined self-built varied-input regime.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent runs run_tests.sh (correctness + cycles) after nearly every semantic change and additionally builds isolated micro-tests to confirm individual transforms (multiply_add fusion, binary selection, hazard-tracking scheduler) preserve semantics before integration, plus reasons about and catches VLIW-specific corruption — placing it above anchor 5 and into anchor-8 territory for transform isolation. However, it leans on the provided test for randomized-input robustness rather than constructing its own diff-against-reference on self-generated varied/edge inputs, and the verification is opportunistic amid heavy thrashing rather than a fully disciplined regime, so it stops short of 8-10. Level 7 reflects strong, frequent, transform-isolating verification that doesn't quite reach the systematic self-built varied-input standard.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection

evidence.note: Consistently tracks cycle count with speedup and gap-to-target: 21821/6.8x → 11091/13.3x → 10339/14.3x → 9303/15.9x, and repeatedly restates 'need ~118x' / 'need 8x more' — solid anchor-5 tracking of distance to 1250.
Treats 9303/15.9x as a known-good baseline it can restore to, and attributes it to specific transforms (multiply_add, root-skip, arithmetic wrap) — a rough transform→gain ledger held verbally.
Explicitly names the stall/circling ('going in circles', 'stuck in a loop of writing kernels that fail', 'we've been trying many approaches') — an anchor-8 recognition signal.

Despite recognizing the loop, it keeps re-attempting the same exhausted approaches (level 0-3 selection, 2-way interleave, smart packer), each failing and reverting to 9303; never redirects effectively and never beats its early baseline — grinding, the opposite of anchor-8 redirection.

Uses a quantitative measurement (10582/14x passing; 1.55 valu ops/bundle vs 6 limit) to diagnose the packing bottleneck, showing genuine measured-vs-expected reconciliation even if action didn't follow.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably tracks measured cycles, speedup, and distance to the 1250 target across the whole arc and knows roughly which change bought which gain (anchor 5), and it repeatedly and explicitly recognizes that it is circling/stalled (an anchor-8 signal). However, recognition never converts into effective redirection: for ~90 steps it churns on the same exhausted approaches (level selection, 2-way interleave, smart packer), each failing and reverting to the 9303 baseline, which is precisely the 'churns on exhausted approaches' failure the high anchors warn against. That combination — strong monitoring plus named-but-unbroken thrash — sits between anchors 5 and 8, landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead

evidence.note: After first vectorized attempt breaks, agent diagnoses the real cause (VLIW slots see pre-bundle state; vselect is a flow not valu instruction), reverts to backup, and restructures scheduling — a genuine machine-model correction, not symptom patching.

Pipelined kernel fails with memory out-of-bounds; agent reverts cleanly to the known-working 9303-cycle kernel and resolves to add optimizations one at a time with correctness checks — clean preservation of hard-won correct state.

Repeated specific fault diagnosis and correction: scratch overflow from per-call temp allocation, 4 load slots exceeding the limit of 2, wrong binary-selection pairing, and same-bundle XOR/multiply_add RAW hazard — each correctly identified and addressed.

Agent repeatedly self-acknowledges 'going in circles' / 'stuck in a loop' yet keeps re-attempting the same complex level-selection + VLIW-scheduling approach that keeps failing, and states an incremental plan it seldom actually follows — clear flailing that keeps it below anchor 8.

Strategy-level pivot from error-prone manual scheduling to an automatic smart VLIW packer / hazard-tracking scheduler after recognizing manual scheduling as the recurring failure mode — evidence of adaptation beyond single-transform reverts.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably reverts broken changes to a preserved correct baseline and diagnoses failures with real specificity (RAW hazards, slot limits, selection-pairing bugs), updating its machine model when surprised — clearly meeting anchor 5 and showing some strategy-level pivots toward 8 (switching to an automatic packer). But it never converts its falsified predictions into a stable, re-sequenced plan that lands: it repeatedly, by its own admission, circles back to the same complex approach that keeps failing, so the 'avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing' quality of anchor 8 is not achieved. This places it at a 6 — solid revert-and-diagnose discipline undercut by persistent thrash.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget

evidence.note: Early and repeated derivation of the load-bound floor: 8 loads/block × 32 blocks × 16 rounds = 4096 loads at 2 loads/cycle = 2048 cycles minimum. At step 44 gives an explicit 'Fundamental minimum analysis' and concludes per-element loads cap at ~2048, so node-value sharing is mandatory to break through.

Instruction-count cost models: multiply_add fuses hash stages 0,2,4 (18→12 valu ops); with 6 valu/cycle → ~15 ops/block → 2.5 cyc/block × 512 = 1280 cycles; level pre-loading for levels 0-5 gives ~1245; hybrid model 12*59+5*128 = 1348. Ties slot limits, SIMD width, and round structure to cycle estimates.

Profiles actual generated code: 14930 valu ops / 9606 bundles = 1.55 valu/bundle (vs limit 6), 1676 loads/868 bundles = 1.93/bundle (near limit 2), theoretical min ~2488 bundles if perfectly packed. Diagnoses that dependent chains within a block prevent filling valu slots — critical-path reasoning — motivating multi-block interleaving. Uses measured-vs-floor gap to pick the next transform.
Quantifies savings of candidate transforms before attempting: level pre-loading eliminates ~12 rounds × 32 blocks × 4 = 1536 load cycles, used to justify prioritizing selection over more loads.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently builds explicit quantitative cost models tying instruction counts, slot occupancy (valu:6, load:2), and SIMD width to cycles, derives multiple theoretical lower bounds (2048 load-bound, ~1280 with selection, ~1348 hybrid), and repeatedly uses the gap between measured (9303/10582) and floor to decide which transform to attempt next — squarely matching anchor 8. It goes further at steps 130-131 by profiling actual ops-per-bundle against slot limits and invoking critical-path dependency reasoning to explain under-packing, elements of anchor 10. It stops short of a full 10 because the model kept shifting and it never converged to a confident recognition of near-optimality, so I place it at 9.

rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
